diseases.name: Urinary Tract Infection (Cystitis / Pyelonephritis)
diseases.scientific_name: Acute bacterial cystitis (lower UTI) / acute pyelonephritis (upper UTI)
diseases.urgency_criteria: Lower-tract symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort) without fever correspond to SEE_DOCTOR_SOON. Fever, chills, flank pain or costovertebral angle tenderness, or vomiting suggest pyelonephritis (SEEK_URGENT_CARE), while hypotension, confusion or other signs of sepsis place the presentation in the EMERGENCY tier.
diseases.description: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is bacterial infection of the urinary tract, ranging from infection of the bladder (cystitis, lower UTI) to infection of the renal pelvis and parenchyma (pyelonephritis, upper UTI). It is classified as uncomplicated when it occurs in patients without structural urinary tract abnormalities or significant comorbidity, and complicated otherwise (e.g., catheters, obstruction, diabetes, pregnancy, male sex in many classifications). Escherichia coli causes most community-acquired UTIs. UTI is one of the most common bacterial infections in adult women.
diseases.pathophysiology: Most UTIs arise by ascending infection: uropathogens from the bowel flora colonize the periurethral area and ascend the urethra into the bladder. Uropathogenic E. coli adhere to uroepithelium via fimbriae (adhesins), which allows the organisms to resist clearance by urine flow. Invasion of the bladder mucosa provokes an acute inflammatory response with neutrophil recruitment, producing pyuria and irritative voiding symptoms. Ascent through the ureters to the renal pelvis and parenchyma produces pyelonephritis with systemic inflammation, and bacteria may enter the bloodstream (urosepsis). Host factors that impair urine flow or bladder emptying (obstruction, stones, catheters, incomplete voiding) increase susceptibility.
diseases.clinicopathologic_correlation: Inflammation of the bladder and urethral mucosa explains dysuria, frequency, urgency and suprapubic discomfort, and mucosal injury accounts for hematuria. Neutrophil influx is detected as pyuria and leukocyte esterase, while nitrate reduction by Enterobacterales produces a positive nitrite test. Renal parenchymal infection causes flank pain and costovertebral angle tenderness, and the systemic cytokine response produces fever, chills, nausea and vomiting.
diseases.onset_progression: Cystitis typically develops over hours to a day or two with dysuria and frequency. Pyelonephritis may follow cystitis symptoms or present directly with fever, flank pain and nausea over one to several days. With appropriate antibiotics, symptoms usually improve within about 48 hours; untreated or complicated upper-tract infection may progress to renal abscess, emphysematous pyelonephritis, acute kidney injury or sepsis.
diseases.follow_up_monitoring: Clinical response is expected within about 48 hours of antibiotic therapy; persistence or worsening prompts urine culture review and reassessment for pyelonephritis, resistant organisms or complicating factors. Outpatient pyelonephritis is re-evaluated within 24-48 hours. Imaging (ultrasound or CT) is considered when there is no improvement, suspected obstruction or abscess. Recurrent UTI (commonly defined as 2 or more in 6 months or 3 or more in 12 months) prompts evaluation of risk factors and preventive strategies.
diseases.source_attribution: StatPearls (Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections; Acute Pyelonephritis), NICE NG109, CDC Clinical Overview of UTIs, Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
causes: Escherichia coli (the majority of community-acquired cases)
Klebsiella species
Staphylococcus saprophyticus (young sexually active women)
Proteus mirabilis
Enterococcus species
Enterobacter and other gram-negative bacilli (more frequent in complicated or healthcare-associated UTI)
risk_factors: Sexual intercourse; spermicide or diaphragm use
Incomplete bladder emptying, urinary retention or obstruction (e.g., stones, prostatic enlargement)
recommended_tests: Urine dipstick: leukocyte esterase and nitrite
Urinalysis with microscopy (pyuria, bacteriuria, hematuria)
Urine culture with susceptibility testing (pyelonephritis, men, pregnancy, recurrence, treatment failure or complicated UTI)
Complete blood count and serum creatinine in suspected pyelonephritis
Blood cultures when sepsis is suspected
Renal ultrasound or CT when obstruction, abscess or non-response is suspected
Pregnancy test in women of reproductive age
treatments: Acute uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women: short-course nitrofurantoin (NICE: 3 days; StatPearls: 5-7 days), or trimethoprim-based therapy where local resistance is low; fosfomycin single dose or pivmecillinam are alternatives
Cystitis in men: 7-day antibiotic course (e.g., trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin per NICE), with urine culture; prostatitis considered
Pregnancy: nitrofurantoin for 7 days (avoided at term) or culture-guided beta-lactam; asymptomatic bacteriuria is also treated

Uncomplicated pyelonephritis managed as outpatient: fluoroquinolone for 7 days where community resistance is 10% or less, often after an initial parenteral dose of ceftriaxone; therapy adjusted to culture
Pyelonephritis with sepsis, persistent vomiting, pregnancy, immunocompromise, obstruction or treatment failure: hospital admission with parenteral antibiotics
Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin are not used for pyelonephritis because of inadequate renal tissue levels
Analgesia with paracetamol (ibuprofen as an alternative where suitable)
home_care: Adequate oral fluid intake to avoid dehydration during infection
Simple analgesia for dysuria and suprapubic discomfort
Completion of the prescribed antibiotic course and clinical review if no improvement within 48 hours
Voiding after sexual intercourse is commonly advised in recurrent UTI

prevention.content: Adequate fluid intake, post-coital voiding, avoidance of spermicides in women with recurrent infection, and minimizing unnecessary urinary catheter use.
Early urine testing and prompt treatment of symptomatic infection; screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy to prevent pyelonephritis.

For recurrent UTI: vaginal estrogen in postmenopausal women, cranberry products or D-mannose (modest evidence), and low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis in selected patients; correction of anatomical or functional abnormalities.

emergency_signs: High fever with rigors
Flank pain with persistent vomiting or inability to keep fluids down
Hypotension, tachycardia or signs of sepsis
Confusion or altered mental status (particularly in older adults)
Markedly reduced urine output
UTI symptoms with fever in pregnancy

differentials.distinguishing_feature: Vaginal discharge, odor or itching with external dysuria; frequency and urgency are less prominent
Urethral or vaginal discharge, new sexual partner; pyuria with negative routine urine culture
Colicky flank-to-groin pain with hematuria, often without fever or pyuria unless infected
Men with perineal or pelvic pain, obstructive voiding symptoms and a tender prostate

differentials.condition: Overactive bladder / interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome)
differentials.distinguishing_feature: Chronic frequency, urgency or bladder pain with sterile urine and no pyuria

medicines.note: First-line for acute uncomplicated cystitis; not used for pyelonephritis (poor tissue levels) and avoided when eGFR is below 45 mL/min/1.73 m2 or at term in pregnancy.
Parenteral cephalosporin used as an initial dose or inpatient therapy for pyelonephritis.
Option for pyelonephritis where local resistance is 10% or less; reserved rather than used first-line for cystitis because of resistance and serious adverse effects (tendon, nerve, CNS).
High E. coli resistance limits empiric use; used only when the organism is known to be susceptible (e.g., pregnancy per NICE).
Beta-lactam alternative generally reserved for culture-guided therapy; beta-lactams are less effective than first-line agents for empiric cystitis.
Recommended analgesic for UTI-related pain (NICE).
Alternative analgesic if suitable (NICE); NSAIDs carry renal risk in dehydration or pyelonephritis.

diseases.name: Peptic Ulcer Disease
diseases.scientific_name: Peptic ulcer (gastric ulcer and duodenal ulcer)
diseases.urgency_criteria: Uncomplicated dyspepsia or epigastric pain corresponds to SEE_DOCTOR_SOON, with alarm features (unintentional weight loss, progressive dysphagia, persistent vomiting, iron-deficiency anemia) warranting prompt endoscopic evaluation. Hematemesis, melena, syncope, tachycardia or sudden severe abdominal pain (possible bleeding or perforation) place the presentation in the EMERGENCY tier.
diseases.description: Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is a break in the gastric or duodenal mucosa that extends through the muscularis mucosae. The two dominant causes are Helicobacter pylori infection and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use, including low-dose aspirin. It typically presents with dull or burning epigastric pain, but may be silent until a complication such as bleeding or perforation occurs. Eradication of H. pylori and withdrawal of NSAIDs markedly reduce recurrence.
diseases.pathophysiology: Ulcers result from an imbalance between aggressive factors (gastric acid, pepsin) and mucosal defenses (mucus-bicarbonate layer, prostaglandins, mucosal blood flow, epithelial renewal). H. pylori colonizes the gastric mucosa and causes chronic active gastritis; antral-predominant infection can increase gastrin and acid output and impair duodenal bicarbonate secretion, favoring duodenal ulcers. NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase-1-dependent prostaglandin synthesis, reducing mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow, in addition to causing direct topical injury. Less common causes include acid hypersecretion (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), other ulcerogenic drugs and severe physiological stress. Deep ulcers can erode vessels (bleeding), penetrate the full wall (perforation) or cause scarring and edema at the pylorus (gastric outlet obstruction).
diseases.clinicopathologic_correlation: Acid contact with the ulcer base produces burning epigastric pain; duodenal ulcer pain classically occurs 2-3 hours after meals and at night, whereas gastric ulcer pain may be provoked by eating. Erosion into a submucosal artery produces hematemesis or melena and, with significant blood loss, dizziness and tachycardia, while chronic occult loss causes iron-deficiency anemia and fatigue. Full-thickness perforation releases gastric contents into the peritoneum, producing sudden severe generalized abdominal pain and peritonitis; pyloric scarring causes early satiety and vomiting.
diseases.onset_progression: Symptoms are usually chronic or recurrent over weeks to months, often episodic with symptom-free intervals. NSAID-associated ulcers are frequently painless and may present first with bleeding. Without removal of the cause, ulcers tend to recur; complications (bleeding, perforation, obstruction) can occur abruptly at any stage.
diseases.follow_up_monitoring: Confirmation of H. pylori eradication is recommended in all treated patients, using urea breath test, stool antigen or biopsy performed at least 4 weeks after completion of antibiotics and after proton pump inhibitors have been held for at least 2 weeks (ACG 2024). Symptoms, need for ongoing NSAID or antiplatelet therapy, and hemoglobin in bleeding ulcers are reviewed. Selected gastric ulcers undergo repeat endoscopy to document healing and exclude malignancy.
diseases.source_attribution: StatPearls (Peptic Ulcer Disease), ACG Clinical Guideline on Treatment of H. pylori (2024), NIDDK, Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
causes: Helicobacter pylori infection (implicated in about 90% of duodenal and 70-90% of gastric ulcers per StatPearls)
NSAIDs, including low-dose aspirin
Other ulcerogenic medications (e.g., corticosteroids in combination with NSAIDs, bisphosphonates)
Gastric acid hypersecretion (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome)
Less common: Crohn disease, malignancy, viral infections, severe physiological stress
risk_factors: NSAID or aspirin use, especially high dose, older age or concomitant anticoagulant/antiplatelet/corticosteroid therapy
Previous peptic ulcer or ulcer bleeding
Family history of peptic ulcer disease
recommended_tests: Upper endoscopy (EGD), the diagnostic gold standard, with biopsy of gastric ulcers to exclude malignancy
H. pylori testing: urea breath test, stool antigen, or endoscopic biopsy (rapid urease test/histology)
Complete blood count (anemia) and iron studies
Fasting serum gastrin when Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is suspected (multiple, refractory or atypically located ulcers)
Upright chest radiograph or CT abdomen when perforation is suspected
treatments: Proton pump inhibitor therapy to heal the ulcer and relieve symptoms
H. pylori eradication: optimized bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole) for 14 days is the preferred first-line regimen per ACG 2024
Vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy is an alternative first-line option (ACG 2024)
Clarithromycin-based triple therapy is used only when clarithromycin susceptibility has been demonstrated
Discontinuation of NSAIDs where possible; when continued NSAID or aspirin therapy is required, co-therapy with a PPI
Bleeding ulcer: resuscitation, endoscopic hemostasis and high-dose PPI therapy
Surgery or interventional radiology for perforation, uncontrolled bleeding or refractory gastric outlet obstruction
home_care: Smoking cessation and limitation of alcohol intake
Avoidance of over-the-counter NSAIDs; paracetamol is the usual alternative analgesic
Adherence to the full course of eradication therapy
Recognition of bleeding warning signs such as black stools or vomiting blood

prevention.content: Avoidance of unnecessary NSAID use; PPI co-therapy for high-risk patients who require NSAIDs or low-dose aspirin; testing for and treating H. pylori in appropriate patients.
Endoscopic evaluation of dyspepsia with alarm features, and H. pylori test-and-treat in dyspeptic patients.
Confirmation of H. pylori eradication, long-term PPI co-therapy when antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy must continue after ulcer bleeding, and follow-up endoscopy of selected gastric ulcers.

emergency_signs: Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material
Black, tarry stools
Sudden, severe abdominal pain with a rigid abdomen
Dizziness, fainting, rapid pulse or low blood pressure
Persistent vomiting suggesting gastric outlet obstruction

differentials.distinguishing_feature: Retrosternal heartburn and regurgitation, often postural; endoscopy shows esophagitis rather than ulcer
Similar dyspepsia but no mucosal break on endoscopy
Older age, weight loss, anemia, early satiety; malignant histology on ulcer biopsy
Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with elevated serum lipase or amylase
Epigastric discomfort with cardiovascular risk factors, ischemic ECG changes and elevated troponin
Right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, Murphy sign and gallstones on ultrasound

medicines.note: Proton pump inhibitor for ulcer healing, a component of H. pylori regimens, and prophylaxis with ongoing NSAID or aspirin use.
Component of H. pylori eradication regimens (e.g., vonoprazan-amoxicillin dual therapy).
ACG 2024 advises against clarithromycin triple therapy unless clarithromycin susceptibility has been demonstrated, because resistance sharply lowers eradication rates.
NSAIDs are the second leading cause of peptic ulcers and increase the risk of ulcer bleeding and perforation.
NSAID; impairs prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection and increases ulcer and bleeding risk.
Even low-dose aspirin causes ulcers and bleeding; when required for cardiovascular prevention it is generally continued with PPI co-therapy rather than stopped.
Antiplatelet effect increases the risk and severity of ulcer bleeding.
Anticoagulation increases the risk and severity of bleeding from peptic ulcers.
Systemic corticosteroids are an ulcer risk factor, particularly when combined with NSAIDs.
Preferred analgesic alternative to NSAIDs in patients with peptic ulcer disease.

diseases.name: Essential Hypertension
diseases.urgency_criteria: Elevated readings without symptoms correspond to SEE_DOCTOR_SOON for confirmation and management. Severe elevation (typically above 180/120 mm Hg) with symptoms of acute target-organ injury (chest pain, dyspnea, neurological deficit, confusion, visual disturbance) indicates a hypertensive emergency and places the presentation in the EMERGENCY tier.
diseases.description: Essential (primary) hypertension is persistently elevated arterial blood pressure without an identifiable secondary cause, accounting for the large majority of hypertension cases. WHO and the 2020 Philippine guidelines define hypertension as office blood pressure of 140/90 mm Hg or higher on repeated measurement, while the ACC/AHA uses 130/80 mm Hg. Most cases are asymptomatic and detected incidentally, so symptom-based recognition is unreliable; headache, dizziness or blurred vision occur mainly with severe elevation. It is a major modifiable risk factor for stroke, coronary heart disease, heart failure and chronic kidney disease.
diseases.pathophysiology: Essential hypertension is multifactorial, arising from interaction of genetic susceptibility with environmental factors such as high sodium intake, obesity and physical inactivity. Increased renal sodium retention expands intravascular volume, while inappropriate activity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system promotes vasoconstriction and further sodium retention. Heightened sympathetic nervous system activity raises heart rate, cardiac output and vascular tone. Over time, vascular remodeling and endothelial dysfunction increase total peripheral resistance, which sustains the elevated pressure. Chronic pressure load causes target-organ damage including left ventricular hypertrophy, arteriolosclerosis, nephrosclerosis and retinopathy.
diseases.clinicopathologic_correlation: Because the pressure rise is gradual and autoregulation adapts, most patients have no symptoms until target organs are damaged. Increased afterload leads to left ventricular hypertrophy (detected on ECG or echocardiography) and eventually heart failure, while arteriolar injury produces retinopathy, albuminuria and declining eGFR. Abrupt severe elevation can overwhelm cerebral autoregulation (encephalopathy with headache, confusion and visual disturbance) or precipitate acute pulmonary edema and myocardial ischemia.
diseases.onset_progression: Typically develops gradually in mid to later adulthood, with prevalence rising steeply with age. It is a lifelong condition that is controlled rather than cured; untreated, it progressively damages the heart, brain, kidneys and retina over years, and acute hypertensive crises may occur at any stage.
diseases.follow_up_monitoring: Diagnosis is confirmed by repeated office readings on separate occasions, ideally supplemented by home or ambulatory monitoring. After starting or changing therapy, blood pressure is reassessed at intervals (response to a regimen is typically judged over several weeks) until target is reached, then periodically. Electrolytes and creatinine/eGFR are checked after initiating RAAS blockers or diuretics, and target-organ status (urine albumin, ECG, lipids, glucose) is reviewed periodically.
diseases.source_attribution: StatPearls (Essential Hypertension; Antihypertensive Medications; Hypertensive Crisis), WHO Hypertension fact sheet, 2020 Philippine Clinical Practice Guidelines for Hypertension, Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
causes: Multifactorial: genetic predisposition combined with environmental and lifestyle factors (no single identifiable cause by definition)
High dietary sodium intake and salt sensitivity
Overweight and obesity
Physical inactivity
Excess alcohol intake
risk_factors: Unhealthy diet high in salt and low in fruits and vegetables
Diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease
recommended_tests: Repeated office blood pressure measurement on at least two separate occasions
Home or 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (identifies white-coat and masked hypertension)
12-lead ECG (left ventricular hypertrophy, arrhythmia)
Serum electrolytes, creatinine and eGFR
Fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipid panel
Urinalysis and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
Fundoscopy for hypertensive retinopathy
treatments: Lifestyle modification for all patients: sodium restriction, DASH-type diet, weight reduction, regular aerobic exercise, limitation of alcohol and smoking cessation
First-line drug classes: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and thiazide or thiazide-like diuretics
Initial two-drug combination (RAAS inhibitor plus calcium channel blocker or diuretic), preferably as a single-pill combination, when BP is well above target (Philippine 2020 CPG: above 150/90 mm Hg)
Philippine 2020 CPG target: below 130/80 mm Hg for most adults; below 140/90 mm Hg for adults aged 80 and older
Resistant hypertension: spironolactone is the preferred fourth-line agent
Beta-blockers reserved for compelling indications (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, post-myocardial infarction, rate control in atrial fibrillation)
Hypertensive emergency: hospital management with controlled BP reduction (generally no more than 25% within the first hour)
home_care: Reduced salt intake and a diet rich in fruits, vegetables and low-fat dairy (DASH pattern)
At least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity physical activity
Weight reduction in overweight individuals
Smoking cessation and moderation of alcohol intake
Home blood pressure monitoring with a validated device
Long-term adherence to prescribed antihypertensive therapy

prevention.content: Population-wide salt reduction, healthy diet, regular physical activity, healthy body weight, and avoidance of tobacco and harmful alcohol use.
Regular blood pressure screening of adults to detect the large proportion of people unaware of their hypertension, with confirmation by repeated or out-of-office readings.

Sustained BP control to target, management of coexisting cardiovascular risk factors (diabetes, dyslipidemia, smoking), and monitoring for target-organ damage to prevent stroke, heart failure and kidney disease.

emergency_signs: Severe headache with markedly elevated blood pressure
Chest pain or pressure
Shortness of breath or breathlessness lying flat
Blurred vision or other visual disturbance
Confusion, drowsiness or seizures
One-sided weakness, facial droop or difficulty speaking

differentials.distinguishing_feature: Elevated office readings with normal home or ambulatory blood pressure

differentials.condition: Secondary hypertension (e.g., primary aldosteronism, renovascular disease, pheochromocytoma, obstructive sleep apnea)
differentials.distinguishing_feature: Young or abrupt onset, resistant hypertension, unprovoked hypokalemia, episodic symptoms or suggestive clinical features
Temporal association with NSAIDs, corticosteroids, decongestants or other pressor agents

differentials.condition: Transient elevation from pain or anxiety
differentials.distinguishing_feature: Resolves when the provoking stimulus is removed; normal repeat readings

medicines.note: First-line dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker; peripheral edema is the common adverse effect.
First-line ARB; monitor potassium and creatinine; contraindicated in pregnancy.
First-line ACE inhibitor; cough, angioedema and hyperkalemia possible; contraindicated in pregnancy.
First-line thiazide diuretic; may cause hypokalemia, hyperglycemia and hyperuricemia.
Preferred fourth-line agent for resistant hypertension; hyperkalemia risk, especially with ACE inhibitors/ARBs or reduced eGFR.
Not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension; used for compelling indications such as HFrEF, post-MI or atrial fibrillation rate control.
Loop diuretic not first-line for hypertension alone; preferred when eGFR is below 30 or with volume overload/heart failure.
NSAIDs can raise blood pressure, reduce antihypertensive efficacy and increase hyperkalemia risk with RAAS inhibitors.
NSAID; same blood pressure and renal cautions as other NSAIDs.
Systemic glucocorticoids cause sodium and fluid retention and can raise blood pressure.

diseases.name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
diseases.urgency_criteria: Symptomatic hyperglycemia (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) or abnormal screening glucose corresponds to SEE_DOCTOR_SOON. Confusion, drowsiness, severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing or very high glucose (possible hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state or ketoacidosis), or severe hypoglycemia on treatment place the presentation in the EMERGENCY tier.
diseases.description: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder of hyperglycemia caused by insulin resistance combined with progressive pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction. It is the most common form of diabetes (over 90% of cases) and is strongly associated with overweight, physical inactivity and family history. It often develops silently over years and may be diagnosed on screening or after complications appear. Long-term hyperglycemia damages small and large blood vessels, causing retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy and cardiovascular disease.
diseases.pathophysiology: Insulin resistance in muscle, liver and adipose tissue reduces peripheral glucose uptake and fails to suppress hepatic glucose production. Beta cells initially compensate by increasing insulin secretion, but progressive beta-cell dysfunction and loss lead to relative insulin deficiency and overt hyperglycemia. Contributing mechanisms include adipose tissue inflammation and increased free fatty acids, reduced incretin (GLP-1) effect, dysregulated glucagon secretion and increased renal glucose reabsorption. Residual insulin secretion usually suppresses ketogenesis, so ketoacidosis is less common than in type 1 diabetes, but marked hyperglycemia can cause a hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. Chronic hyperglycemia drives microvascular and macrovascular injury.
diseases.clinicopathologic_correlation: When blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold, glycosuria causes osmotic diuresis (polyuria) and consequent dehydration and thirst (polydipsia). Loss of glucose calories and catabolism can produce weight loss and fatigue, and osmotic changes in the lens cause fluctuating blurred vision. Hyperglycemia impairs immune function and wound healing, increasing infections such as UTI and candidiasis. Severe hyperosmolality leads to confusion and reduced consciousness in the hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.
diseases.onset_progression: Insidious onset, typically in adulthood, often preceded by years of prediabetes; many patients are asymptomatic at diagnosis. The disease is progressive, with declining beta-cell function commonly requiring intensification of therapy over time. Microvascular and macrovascular complications accumulate with duration and degree of hyperglycemia.
diseases.follow_up_monitoring: HbA1c every 3-6 months (at least twice yearly when at target, more often after therapy changes). Blood pressure at each visit; lipid profile periodically. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR at least annually. Dilated retinal examination at diagnosis and periodically thereafter, and comprehensive foot examination at least annually. Self-monitoring of glucose is used especially with insulin or sulfonylurea therapy.
diseases.source_attribution: StatPearls (Type 2 Diabetes), WHO Diabetes fact sheet, CDC Type 2 Diabetes, ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026, Williams Textbook of Endocrinology
causes: Insulin resistance (skeletal muscle, liver, adipose tissue)
Progressive pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction
Reduced incretin effect and dysregulated glucagon secretion
Genetic predisposition interacting with obesity and physical inactivity
risk_factors: Overweight or obesity, especially abdominal adiposity
Prediabetes (impaired fasting glucose or impaired glucose tolerance)
Polycystic ovary syndrome; Asian and certain other ethnic ancestries
recommended_tests: HbA1c (diagnostic at 6.5% or higher, 48 mmol/mol)
Fasting plasma glucose (diagnostic at 126 mg/dL or higher, 7.0 mmol/L)
75-g oral glucose tolerance test (2-hour value 200 mg/dL or higher, 11.1 mmol/L)
Random plasma glucose 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms
Serum creatinine/eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
Lipid profile
Dilated retinal examination and foot examination (monofilament)
Serum or urine ketones and serum osmolality when DKA or hyperosmolar state is suspected
treatments: Lifestyle therapy (medical nutrition therapy, physical activity, weight management) as the foundation of care
Metformin as the usual initial pharmacological agent
SGLT2 inhibitors (and/or GLP-1 receptor agonists) for patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure or chronic kidney disease, independent of HbA1c
Additional agents (sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, pioglitazone, insulin) chosen by efficacy, hypoglycemia risk, weight effect, cost and comorbidities
Insulin when hyperglycemia is severe or symptomatic, or when catabolic features are present
Cardiovascular risk reduction: blood pressure control, statin therapy, and ACE inhibitor or ARB when albuminuria and hypertension coexist
Individualized glycemic targets (an HbA1c below 7% is appropriate for many non-pregnant adults), avoiding hypoglycemia
home_care: Healthy eating pattern with portion control and limitation of added sugars and refined carbohydrates
At least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity physical activity
Weight reduction in overweight individuals
Smoking cessation
Self-monitoring of blood glucose when indicated, and recognition of hypoglycemia symptoms
Daily foot inspection and appropriate footwear

prevention.content: Maintenance of healthy weight, regular physical activity and healthy diet; structured lifestyle programs in people with prediabetes can prevent or delay type 2 diabetes.
Screening of at-risk adults (e.g., overweight adults with risk factors, adults 35 years or older) with HbA1c, fasting glucose or OGTT for early detection.
Glycemic, blood pressure and lipid control, and regular screening of eyes, kidneys and feet to prevent or slow retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, amputation and cardiovascular events.

emergency_signs: Confusion, drowsiness or reduced consciousness
Severe dehydration with extreme thirst and very high blood glucose
Persistent vomiting, abdominal pain or rapid deep breathing (possible ketoacidosis)
Symptoms of severe hypoglycemia (sweating, tremor, confusion, seizures) in patients on insulin or sulfonylureas
Chest pain or stroke symptoms
Rapidly spreading foot infection or gangrene

differentials.condition: Type 1 diabetes / latent autoimmune diabetes in adults
differentials.distinguishing_feature: Often leaner, prone to ketosis, positive islet autoantibodies and low C-peptide
Temporal relation to glucocorticoids, antipsychotics or other diabetogenic drugs
Accompanying hormonal features such as cushingoid habitus or acral growth

differentials.condition: Pancreatogenic diabetes (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, hemochromatosis)
differentials.distinguishing_feature: History of pancreatic disease, steatorrhea or iron overload
Young onset, strong autosomal dominant family history, often without obesity

medicines.note: Usual first-line agent; low hypoglycemia risk; contraindicated when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.
SGLT2 inhibitor with cardiorenal benefit in heart failure and CKD; genital mycotic infection and euglycemic ketoacidosis are recognized risks.
Effective and inexpensive sulfonylurea but carries hypoglycemia risk, particularly in older adults, renal impairment or missed meals.
Statin therapy is recommended for cardiovascular risk reduction in most adults with diabetes.
ARB preferred for hypertension with albuminuria in diabetes to slow kidney disease progression.
ACE inhibitor preferred for hypertension with albuminuria in diabetes; not combined with an ARB.
Systemic glucocorticoids raise blood glucose and can destabilize glycemic control.
Beta-blockers can mask adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia (e.g., tremor, palpitations).

diseases.name: Bronchial Asthma
diseases.urgency_criteria: Intermittent wheeze, cough or chest tightness responding to reliever therapy corresponds to SEE_DOCTOR_SOON for diagnosis and controller therapy. An exacerbation with inability to speak in full sentences, respiratory rate above 30/min, heart rate above 120/min, SpO2 below 90%, PEF 50% of predicted or less, drowsiness, confusion or a silent chest places the presentation in the EMERGENCY tier.
diseases.description: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways characterized by variable, often reversible expiratory airflow limitation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. It presents with episodic wheeze, shortness of breath, chest tightness and cough that vary over time and in intensity, often worse at night, with exercise or with viral infections. It affects all ages, cannot be cured, but is well controlled in most people with inhaled corticosteroid-containing treatment. Severe exacerbations can be fatal.
diseases.pathophysiology: In type 2 (allergic/eosinophilic) asthma, allergen exposure in sensitized individuals triggers IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation with release of histamine, leukotrienes and other mediators, causing early-phase bronchoconstriction. Th2 lymphocytes produce IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13, which promote IgE synthesis, eosinophil recruitment and survival, and mucus hypersecretion, driving the late-phase inflammatory response. Airway hyperresponsiveness results from increased smooth muscle mass and contractility, mediator release and neural mechanisms, so that non-specific triggers (cold air, exercise, smoke) provoke bronchoconstriction. Chronic inflammation leads to airway remodeling with basement membrane thickening, smooth muscle hypertrophy and subepithelial fibrosis, which can cause fixed airflow obstruction. Non-type 2 (T2-low) phenotypes also exist, with neutrophilic or paucigranulocytic inflammation.
diseases.clinicopathologic_correlation: Bronchial smooth muscle constriction, mucosal edema and mucus plugging narrow the airways, producing expiratory wheeze, dyspnea and chest tightness, with reduced FEV1 and FEV1/FVC on spirometry. Reversibility of this narrowing with a bronchodilator (an FEV1 increase of 12% or more and 200 mL or more) reflects its largely functional basis. Circadian variation in airway tone and inflammation explains nocturnal cough and symptoms. In severe exacerbations, airflow becomes so limited that breath sounds diminish (silent chest) and hypoxemia and hypercapnia produce drowsiness or confusion.
diseases.onset_progression: Often begins in childhood but can start at any age, including adult-onset and occupational asthma. The course is variable, with periods of good control interrupted by exacerbations commonly triggered by viral respiratory infections, allergens, smoke, pollution or poor adherence to controller therapy. Poorly controlled long-standing asthma may progress to persistent airflow limitation due to remodeling.
diseases.follow_up_monitoring: Review 1-3 months after starting treatment and then every 3-12 months, assessing symptom control, exacerbation risk factors, lung function (spirometry or PEF), inhaler technique, adherence and side effects (GINA). After an exacerbation, follow-up within 2-7 days for adults and adolescents. Every patient should have a written asthma action plan; treatment is stepped up or down according to control.
diseases.source_attribution: GINA 2025 Summary Guide, StatPearls (Asthma; Pathophysiology of Asthma), WHO Asthma fact sheet, Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
causes: Chronic airway inflammation with bronchial hyperresponsiveness arising from genetic predisposition and environmental exposures
Allergic sensitization (atopy) to aeroallergens such as house dust mite, pollen, animal dander and molds
Occupational sensitizers (occupational asthma)
Exacerbation triggers: viral respiratory infections, allergens, tobacco smoke, air pollution, cold air, exercise, and certain medicines (beta-blockers; NSAIDs/aspirin in susceptible individuals)
risk_factors: Family history of asthma or atopy
Early-life exposures: prematurity/low birth weight, maternal smoking, tobacco smoke and air pollution
Occupational exposure to sensitizers or irritants
Viral respiratory infections in early childhood
recommended_tests: Spirometry with bronchodilator responsiveness testing (FEV1 increase of 12% or more and 200 mL or more in adults)
Peak expiratory flow variability monitoring
Bronchial challenge testing when spirometry is non-diagnostic
Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) and blood eosinophil count for type 2 inflammation
Allergy testing (skin prick or specific IgE) to identify relevant triggers
Chest radiograph to exclude alternative diagnoses when atypical
Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas in severe exacerbations
treatments: All adults and adolescents receive inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-containing treatment; SABA-only treatment is not recommended (GINA)
GINA Track 1 (preferred): as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol as reliever, with maintenance-and-reliever ICS-formoterol at higher steps
GINA Track 2 (alternative): daily maintenance ICS or ICS-LABA with as-needed SABA or ICS-SABA reliever

Step-up options for uncontrolled asthma: higher-dose ICS-LABA, add-on long-acting muscarinic antagonist, and phenotype-directed biologics (anti-IgE, anti-IL-5/5R, anti-IL-4R, anti-TSLP) for severe asthma
Acute exacerbation: repeated inhaled SABA (pMDI with spacer) or ICS-formoterol, controlled oxygen to target saturation, and oral prednisolone/prednisone 40-50 mg daily for 5-7 days in adults
Management of comorbidities (allergic rhinitis, obesity, GERD, obstructive sleep apnea)
home_care: Correct inhaler technique, checked at every opportunity, with use of a spacer for pMDIs where appropriate
Written asthma action plan for recognizing and responding to worsening symptoms
Avoidance of tobacco smoke and identified allergen or occupational triggers
Regular physical activity
Up-to-date respiratory vaccinations (influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal and others per GINA)

prevention.content: Avoidance of tobacco smoke exposure in pregnancy and early life, reduction of air pollution exposure, and control of occupational sensitizer exposure.
Early objective diagnosis with spirometry in people with recurrent wheeze, cough or dyspnea, and early initiation of ICS-containing therapy.

Regular ICS-containing controller or anti-inflammatory reliever therapy, trigger avoidance, written action plans, vaccination and prompt treatment of exacerbations to prevent severe attacks and airway remodeling.

emergency_signs: Breathlessness at rest or inability to speak in full sentences
Use of accessory muscles, respiratory rate above 30/min or heart rate above 120/min
Oxygen saturation below 90% or cyanosis
Drowsiness, confusion or exhaustion
Silent chest (inaudible breath sounds)
Poor or no response to repeated reliever doses

differentials.distinguishing_feature: Older smoker or exposure history, progressive dyspnea and post-bronchodilator airflow limitation that is not fully reversible
Orthopnea, peripheral edema, basal crackles, elevated natriuretic peptides and cardiac dysfunction on echocardiography
Inspiratory stridor and throat tightness with normal lung function between episodes
Chronic daily purulent sputum and recurrent chest infections; dilated airways on CT
Sudden onset after choking episode with localized, often unilateral wheeze
Fever, focal crackles and consolidation on chest radiograph

medicines.note: GINA Track 1 preferred reliever (as-needed low-dose) and maintenance-and-reliever therapy; reduces severe exacerbations versus SABA-based regimens.
Short-acting reliever and first-line bronchodilator in acute exacerbations; SABA-only treatment without ICS is not recommended.
Short oral course (40-50 mg daily for 5-7 days in adults) for exacerbations; repeated or long-term use carries significant systemic adverse effects.
Beta-blockers can cause asthma symptoms or exacerbations (GINA); beta-1 selective agents carry lower risk and are used only with a strong indication and close supervision.
Can precipitate severe bronchospasm in aspirin/NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease; previous reactions are asked about before prescribing.
NSAID; avoided in patients with a history of NSAID-induced bronchospasm.
NSAID; same precaution regarding NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease.
